summary: Verified mathematical dossier for a 94-second film: a vertical torus with four nondegenerate critical points, exact sublevel and cross-section geometry, and Euler characteristic 1−2+1=0.
content:
Use the following explicit construction; the calculations are independent derivations for this film.

Let R=2, r=0.8, and let u,v be angles modulo 2π. Define
T(u,v)=((R+r cos v)cos u, r sin v, (R+r cos v)sin u).
Its major circle lies in the vertical xz-plane. Write ρ(v)=R+r cos v, so 1.2≤ρ≤2.8. The surface satisfies
(√(x²+z²)−R)²+y²=r².
Since |T_u|=ρ, |T_v|=r, and T_u·T_v=0, the parametrization is regular everywhere. Recovering u from (x,z) and v from (ρ−R,y) shows that it is an embedded torus after periodic seam identification. Its bounds are x,z∈[−2.8,2.8], y∈[−0.8,0.8].

Define height h:T²→ℝ by h(x,y,z)=z and the included surface by M_a={p∈T²:h(p)≤a}. A critical point has zero height derivative in every tangent direction. A Morse function has nonsingular Hessian at every critical point; its index is the number of negative Hessian eigenvalues in local coordinates. Thus index 0 means minimum, index 1 saddle, and index 2 maximum. These definitions agree with [Milnor, §2](https://math.stanford.edu/~ralph/math215b/Milnor.pdf).

Here h(u,v)=ρ(v)sin u, with
h_u=ρ cos u, h_v=−r sin v sin u,
H=[[−ρ sin u,−r sin v cos u],[−r sin v cos u,−r cos v sin u]].
Because ρ>0, criticality forces cos u=0 and then sin v=0. There are exactly four points:

| Point (u,v) | Position | Height | Coordinate Hessian diagonal | Index |
|---|---|---:|---|---:|
| (3π/2,0) | (0,0,−2.8) | −2.8 | (2.8,0.8) | 0 |
| (3π/2,π) | (0,0,−1.2) | −1.2 | (1.2,−0.8) | 1 |
| (π/2,π) | (0,0,1.2) | 1.2 | (−1.2,0.8) | 1 |
| (π/2,0) | (0,0,2.8) | 2.8 | (−2.8,−0.8) | 2 |

The determinants are 2.24, −0.96, −0.96, 2.24. All are nonzero. Coordinate Hessian magnitudes are not physical curvatures; their inertia determines the index.

At the lower saddle, Taylor expansion gives h≈−1.2+0.6δu²−0.4δv²; at the upper saddle h≈1.2−0.6δu²+0.4δv². For exact directional demonstrations, highlight short arcs T(u_c+t,v_c) and T(u_c,v_c+t), |t|≤0.35. One rises away from each saddle while the other descends. These are curves on the actual torus; any quadratic inset must be labeled a local model.

For the geometry engine, the following gives the entire included surface without filling a solid. Let θ=u+π/2, so h=−ρ cos θ. For each admissible v, set
α(v,a)=acos(clamp(−a/ρ(v),−1,1)),
u=−π/2+wα(v,a), −1≤w≤1.
Map (w,v) through T. If −2.8<a<−1.2, use v∈[−β,β], β=acos((−a−2)/0.8). If −1.2≤a<2.8, use v∈[−π,π], retaining the clamped α. Where a≥ρ, α=π covers the complete u-circle. For a<−2.8 the set is empty; at a=−2.8 it is one point; for a≥2.8 use the complete torus. Collapsed parameter edges and periodic seams are identifications, not physical boundaries. This construction can be tessellated into reusable patches; avoid treating patch-center color thresholds as exact clipping.

The gold waterline is C_a=T²∩{z=a}. Its exact branches are
C_a^±(v)=(±√(ρ(v)²−a²), r sin v, a).
For |a|<1.2, each sign is a separate closed loop with v∈[−π,π]. For 1.2<|a|<2.8, use v∈[−β,β], β=acos((|a|−2)/0.8): traverse the plus branch forward and the minus branch backward to form ONE closed loop. The endpoints coincide at x=0. At |a|=1.2 the level is a figure-eight with a saddle crossing; it is not a regular boundary manifold. At |a|=2.8 it is a point; outside that range it is empty. Clamp square roots only against roundoff after enforcing admissibility. Sample more densely near joining endpoints.

Worked sections: at a=0, the two loops are circles (±(2+0.8 cos v),0.8 sin v,0). At a=±2.4, β=π/3; the branch midpoints have x=±√2.08≈±1.442221, y=0, and joining endpoints have x=0, y=±√0.48≈±0.692820. A scanning plane patch (s,t,a), s∈[−3.2,3.2], t∈[−1.2,1.2], covers the object.

The compactness and smoothness hypotheses hold. Between critical values, sublevels are diffeomorphic; crossing one nondegenerate point adds a cell of its index up to homotopy. Surface handles realize these transitions geometrically. These statements follow from [Milnor, Theorems 3.1, 3.2 and 3.5](https://math.stanford.edu/~ralph/math215b/Milnor.pdf).

| Regular height | Surface type | Boundary curves | χ |
|---|---|---:|---:|
| a<−2.8 | Empty | 0 | 0 |
| −2.8<a<−1.2 | Disk | 1 | 1 |
| −1.2<a<1.2 | Cylinder/annulus S¹×[0,1] | 2 | 0 |
| 1.2<a<2.8 | Torus with one open disk removed | 1 | −1 |
| a>2.8 | Closed torus | 0 | 0 |

The lower saddle attaches an untwisted band to two arcs of the disk boundary, making an annulus. The upper saddle joins the annulus’s two boundary components with another band, producing genus one with one boundary. The maximum caps that boundary. Connectedness is retained throughout. For these connected orientable surfaces, χ=2−2g−b independently confirms the table.

Define Euler characteristic as χ=V−E+F for a finite triangulation, independent of triangulation. Define m_k as the number of index-k critical points. A k-cell contributes (−1)^k, so the four contributions are +1,−1,−1,+1. Consequently χ(T²)=m₀−m₁+m₂=1−2+1=0. Milnor’s [§3 cell theorem and §6 Application 2](https://math.stanford.edu/~ralph/math215b/Milnor.pdf) justify this relation.

Teaching safeguards: M_a is a two-dimensional surface subset, not the three-dimensional liquid beneath the plane. At regular levels, C_a=∂M_a is one-dimensional. Boundary count does not determine surface topology: disk and punctured torus both have one boundary. A horizontal donut with height r sin v has critical circles and fails the Morse condition. Use regular levels for stable surface labels. Do not describe a band as merely adding another boundary curve, or the cell theorem as literal equality with a graph.

For the approved 94-second structure, reserve 0–14s for height and M_a; 14–27s for the minimum; 27–46s and 46–65s for the saddles; 65–77s for the cap; 77–94s for Euler counting and the final relation. Encode included surface in teal/cyan, intersections in gold, extrema in coral, and saddles in violet. Keep one main fixed-screen MathTex formula at a time. The derivative calculation establishes Morse criticality; the cited theorem establishes the Euler conclusion. The rendered sweep illustrates the attachments and must still undergo continuous-video review.

Evaluated 3,609 cross-section samples across nine heights, including both saddles. Maximum residual in (sqrt(x²+z²)−2)²+y²−0.64 was 1.111×10⁻¹⁵. An initial PowerShell run had parsing and numeric-overload errors; its results were discarded and the corrected run used explicit floating-point arguments.

Independent JavaScript clipping of a periodic 128×64 triangulated torus at heights −3, −2.4, 0.15, 2.4, 3 gave Euler characteristics 0,1,0,−1,0 and boundary counts 0,1,2,1,0. Nonempty regular boundaries all had vertex degree two. This is a discretized consistency check, not a proof.
Read Milnor’s original text through Stanford’s PDF: torus example in §1; critical point and index definitions in §2; Theorems 3.1, 3.2, 3.5; Euler relation in §6.
